Road Traffic Act 1994

Alcohol limits, driving licence categories, penalties, fitness to drive — the key provisions from the Wegenverkeerswet 1994 that every candidate must know.

  • Alcohol & Drugs
  • Licence Categories
  • Penalties
  • Fitness to Drive
  • Probationary Period

The Wegenverkeerswet 1994 (Road Traffic Act) is the primary Dutch traffic law — the RVV 1990 is a regulation issued under it. While the RVV covers how you must behave on the road, the Wegenverkeerswet covers who may drive, what happens when rules are broken, and what physical and mental standards drivers must meet.

This supplement covers the parts of the Wegenverkeerswet most relevant to the theory exam: alcohol and drug limits, licence categories, the penalty system and the probationary driving period for new licence holders.

Alcohol & Drug Limits

The legal blood alcohol levels in the Netherlands — and what happens when they are exceeded.

The General Limit 0.5 ‰ BAC

The standard blood alcohol limit for drivers in the Netherlands is 0.5 ‰ (permille) blood alcohol content (BAC). This is equivalent to approximately 220 µg/l (micrograms per litre) in exhaled breath, measured by a breathalyser.

Driving above 0.5 ‰ is a criminal offence. Below 0.5 ‰ you are legally permitted to drive — but alcohol impairs judgement and reaction time well before the legal limit. The safe choice is always zero alcohol before driving.

Lower Limit for New Drivers 0.2 ‰

Drivers who have held their licence for five years or less are subject to a lower limit of 0.2 ‰. This applies automatically from the date the licence is issued until exactly five years later. The lower limit is part of the Dutch approach to novice driver safety — new drivers are statistically at higher risk and benefit from stricter alcohol rules.

Professional drivers — taxi drivers, bus drivers, truck drivers — are also subject to the 0.2 ‰ limit when driving in their professional capacity.

In practice, 0.2 ‰ is so close to zero that even a small glass of beer can bring a new driver above the limit. The safest approach for new drivers is complete abstinence from alcohol before driving.
Drugs and Medication Zero tolerance for drugs

Dutch law prohibits driving under the influence of substances that impair driving ability. For a defined list of illegal drugs — including THC (cannabis), cocaine, MDMA, heroin and others — zero-tolerance limits apply. Any detectable amount above the threshold for these substances is a criminal offence.

For prescription medication that may affect driving ability — such as strong painkillers, sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medication and some antihistamines — the driver must assess with their doctor whether they are fit to drive. There is no fixed blood level limit for prescribed medication, but driving while impaired by medication is still an offence.

Many medicines carry a warning label with a car symbol indicating that driving may be affected. Always check before driving when starting a new medication.
What Happens If You Are Over the Limit

Being caught driving over the alcohol limit results in: immediate suspension of the right to drive, a fine (which increases with BAC level), possible criminal prosecution, possible mandatory referral to the CBR for a fitness assessment, and — for serious cases — a requirement to complete an educational course (EMA — Educatieve Maatregel Alcohol) before the licence is returned. Repeat offenders face licence revocation.

Driving Licence Categories

Which licence you need for which vehicle — and the age requirements for each.

The Dutch Licence System Rijbewijs

The Dutch driving licence system follows the European Union standard categories. Each category entitles the holder to drive specific types of vehicles. Driving a vehicle for which you do not hold the appropriate category is a criminal offence — not merely an administrative one.

Licences are issued by the CBR (Centraal Bureau Rijvaardigheidsbewijzen) and are valid for a set period depending on the holder's age.

Accompanied Driving — 2toDrive (2vM)

In the Netherlands, 17-year-olds may drive a standard car with a qualified accompanying adult through the 2toDrive (2vM) programme. The accompanying person must be registered, hold a valid B licence, and be at least 27 years old. The young driver may drive anywhere in the Netherlands under these conditions until their 18th birthday, when they can take the standard test. This is a popular route as it provides far more driving experience before the test.

Licence Validity Period Expiry rules

Dutch driving licences are not permanently valid — they must be renewed periodically:

  • Category B (car) for drivers under 70: valid for 10 years
  • Category B for drivers 70 and over: valid for 5 years, then 1 year increments after 75
  • Professional categories (C, D and derived): valid for 5 years, requiring periodic medical checks
  • AM (moped): valid for 10 years

Driving with an expired licence is treated the same as driving without a licence — a serious offence.

The Penalty System

How traffic violations are punished — fines, licence sanctions and criminal prosecution.

Fines — The WAHV System Administrative fines

Most everyday traffic violations in the Netherlands are handled through the WAHV (Wet Administratiefrechtelijke Handhaving Verkeersvoorschriften) — the administrative traffic law enforcement system. Under WAHV, fines are issued without going to court. You receive a fine notice and can pay it, contest it, or — if you disagree — appeal through an administrative procedure.

WAHV fines cover violations such as speeding, running red lights, illegal parking, mobile phone use while driving and many others. The fine amounts are set nationally and published in the official WAHV tariff list, which is updated periodically.

Speeding fines

Fine amount increases with speed above the limit. Minor excess (1–10 km/h) attracts modest fines. Large excess (30+ km/h over) can result in licence confiscation on the spot and criminal prosecution.

Red light violation

Running a red traffic light is one of the higher WAHV fines. Cameras at major intersections record violations automatically. The fine applies even if no other vehicle was present.

Mobile phone while driving

Using a handheld phone while driving — for any purpose — attracts a significant fine. This applies to cyclists too. The fine for cyclists is lower than for car drivers but still substantial.

No seatbelt

Not wearing a seatbelt, or allowing a passenger under 18 to travel without proper restraint, results in a fine. The driver is responsible for all passengers under 18 being properly buckled.

Illegal parking

Parking in a prohibited location — including on yellow lines, at bus stops, in disabled bays without a card, or on crossings — results in a fine and possible vehicle removal (wegslepen) at the owner's expense.

Criminal offences

Serious violations — high-level speeding, drink-driving above 0.8 ‰, hit-and-run, dangerous driving — move beyond WAHV into criminal law. These are prosecuted in court and can result in imprisonment and permanent licence revocation.

Licence Confiscation on the Spot Invordering rijbewijs

In serious cases, a police officer can confiscate your driving licence immediately on the roadside. This happens when the officer determines that allowing you to continue driving poses an unacceptable risk to public safety. Grounds include:

  • Alcohol level significantly above the limit
  • Speed grossly in excess of the limit (typically 50+ km/h over)
  • Extremely dangerous driving behaviour
  • Driving under the influence of drugs

The confiscation is immediate — you cannot drive away. The licence is then reviewed by the CBR and the public prosecutor's office. You must prove fitness to drive before it is returned.

Fitness to Drive

Medical requirements, vision standards, and when you must report a condition to the CBR.

Medical Fitness Requirements CBR medical assessment

To obtain and retain a driving licence, you must meet minimum medical fitness standards set by the EU and implemented in Dutch law. These cover vision, hearing, physical mobility, neurological conditions, psychiatric conditions, diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

For a standard B licence, no medical examination is required at first application — the applicant self-declares fitness. However, from age 70, a medical check is required at renewal. For professional licence categories (C, D), a medical examination is required every 5 years from the outset.

Vision Requirements Minimum standards

The minimum vision standard for a category B licence is:

  • Visual acuity: at least 0.5 (6/12) in both eyes together, with or without correction (glasses or contact lenses)
  • Visual field: minimum 120 degrees horizontal, with no significant defect in the central 20 degrees
  • Colour vision: no specific requirement for category B — colour blindness alone does not disqualify a driver

If you normally wear glasses or contact lenses to meet the vision standard, you must wear them every time you drive. Driving without corrective lenses when you need them to meet the standard is a violation.

Glasses or contact lenses required for driving are indicated on the licence itself with a code. The code 01.01 means "glasses required". The code 01.02 means "contact lenses required".
Reporting a Medical Condition Your obligation

If you develop a medical condition that may affect your fitness to drive, you have a legal obligation to report it to the CBR. The CBR then assesses whether you remain fit to drive, with or without conditions.

Conditions that typically require reporting include:

  • Epilepsy or seizure disorders
  • Significant vision deterioration
  • Stroke or TIA (mini-stroke)
  • Severe psychiatric disorders
  • Insulin-dependent diabetes with hypoglycaemia risk
  • Heart conditions affecting consciousness
  • Dementia or significant cognitive decline

Failing to report a relevant condition and continuing to drive is a criminal offence — particularly if you are involved in an accident.

Fatigue — A Legal Risk Too

Driving while severely fatigued is treated similarly to driving under the influence in Dutch traffic law. If a police officer determines that a driver is so tired that their ability to drive safely is impaired, they can be ordered to stop driving. Causing an accident while knowingly driving in a severely fatigued state can result in criminal liability for dangerous driving. The law does not set a "fatigue limit" like an alcohol limit — but the duty of care applies equally.

The Probationary Period

Special rules for new licence holders in their first five years.

Five-Year Probationary Period Nieuw rijbewijs

Every new Dutch driving licence holder enters a five-year probationary period from the date their licence is issued. During this period, stricter rules apply:

  • Lower alcohol limit: 0.2 ‰ instead of 0.5 ‰
  • Lower speeding threshold for immediate confiscation: licence can be confiscated at lower excess speeds
  • Higher penalty sensitivity: certain violations during the probationary period can result in mandatory retesting

After five years from the licence issue date, the probationary period ends automatically and the standard limits apply.

EMA — Educational Programme for Alcohol Mandatory course

Drivers caught with a BAC of 1.3 ‰ or above — or who are caught drink-driving twice within five years — are required to complete the EMA (Educatieve Maatregel Alcohol) programme before their licence is returned. This is a mandatory alcohol education course run by the CBR.

The EMA consists of several sessions covering the effects of alcohol, driving behaviour and relapse prevention. Completion is required before the driver can regain their licence. Cost is borne by the driver.

Standard driver (5+ years)
  • Alcohol limit: 0.5 ‰
  • Standard WAHV fine scale
  • Standard licence confiscation thresholds
  • Licence valid for 10 years (under 70)
New driver (0–5 years)
  • Alcohol limit: 0.2 ‰
  • Higher sensitivity to violations
  • Lower thresholds for confiscation
  • Possible mandatory retest for serious violations
Supplement A — What to Take Away

The standard alcohol limit is 0.5 ‰. New drivers (first 5 years) and professional drivers face a lower limit of 0.2 ‰. Drugs have zero-tolerance limits for illegal substances. Licences are category-based — driving without the right category is a criminal offence. The CBR manages licence fitness assessments. Medical conditions affecting driving must be reported. New drivers face a 5-year probationary period with stricter rules throughout.
